newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy, hit by exodus, urges Albanians to stay home.
newsitem.headline: Italy, hit by exodus, urges Albanians to stay home.

text.p: Italy, struggling to cope with an exodus of Albanians fleeing violence at home, said on Sunday that Europe was committed to efforts to rebuild the Balkan state and stem the tide of refugees.

"The crisis will not be resolved by fleeing but by the rebuilding of Albania... Europe will provide the material conditions for this to happen," Prime Minister Romano Prodi told reporters on a flying visit to the southern port of Brindisi.
"This is an emergency situation and the objective is (to convince Albanians) to stay in their homeland."
Prodi said that an EU mission scheduled to visit Tirana on Monday would seek to restore civil order.
Thousands of terrified Albanian refugees have crossed the Adriatic in recent days in an array of old boats to escape the violence engulfing much of their impoverished country.

"We travelled with our hearts in our mouths," said 19-year-old student Kulluri Bardyhxl after he was pulled off one overcrowded ship. Despite sunny weather, coastguards said rough seas appeared to have slowed the pace of arrivals.

The foreign ministry said Albania had asked for a meeting between Prime Minister Bashkim Fino and the European Union to review the situation and said it could take place on March 24, when EU foreign ministers are due to meet in Brussels.

The EU, meeting in the Netherlands at the weekend, said it would send military and police advisers but ruled out military intervention to end the chaos that has swept Albania following the failure in January of fraudulent savings schemes.

The EU mission, led by Dutch diplomat Jan Comte de Marchant et d'Ansembourg with representatives from the Netherlands, Greece, Italy, the European Commission and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), was due to meet in Rome for talks on Monday morning before leaving for Tirana, an Italian foreign ministry spokesman said.

Some 1,600 Albanians crossed in choppy conditions on Saturday night and Sunday morning, including 858 crammed onto a rusting ship who were rescued by coastguards in a dramatic seven-hour operation after their vessel ran aground.
Refugees have been moved to hastily-organised "hospitality centres" set up in schools, offices and barracks and the mayor of Brindisi, Lorenzo Maggi, said his city was being overwhelmed.
"We were ready to accept a more modest-sized exodus. Today the phenomenon is taking on Biblical proportions," he said.
He warned of health and other problems if the exodus continued unabated. "These people are desperate and without hope and they could fall into the clutches of organised crime."

A small protest broke at one centre in Brindisi but officials said calm had been restored and some 250 refugees, each carrying plastic bags full of food, were packed onto buses and taken to other destinations to ease the overcrowding.
